items.question: Put the versions in order, oldest at the top.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort by the minor number, read as a whole number.

byKey.b: You placed 3.10.4 as if it were the decimal 3.1. Its minor number, 10, comes after 9.
byKey.e: You moved 3.13.0 down because of its patch of 0. The minor number, 13, decides first.

items.prose: A PATH lists five folders. A program called `pytest` sits in the fourth folder only.
items.question: When Ana types `pytest`, how many folders does the shell open?

feedback.correct: Folders 1 to 3 hold no `pytest`; folder 4 does, and the search stops.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The shell opens folders in order until it finds a match.

byKey.all: You searched every folder. The shell stops at the first match, in folder 4.
byKey.one: You assumed the shell knows where `pytest` is. It must check folders 1 to 3 first.

explain.text: The shell opens folder 1, 2 and 3 and finds nothing, then finds `pytest` in folder 4 and stops. Only a command that is not found makes it open all five.

You put it last. The end of the PATH is searched last, so `/opt/homebrew/bin` still wins.

items.question: What should she do?

options.text: Go up to `project` with `cd ..`, then run `python3 src/backtest.py`

Python ran the script; the script then looked for the prices in the wrong folder.

explain.text: From `src`, the name means `src/data/prices.csv`, which does not exist. From `project` it points at the real file. Run project scripts from the project's top folder.

items.title: The Stage 0 exit test
items.prose: A share closed at £100.00, £104.00 and £101.92 on three days. A day's return is $(\text{new} - \text{old}) \div \text{old}$. Write `returns.py`. The `def` block names a recipe, `daily_return`, that the script uses twice; you write its one-line answer after `return`. In the example `print`, `{r1 * 100:.2f}` writes `r1` times 100 with two decimals.
items.question: Make `daily_return` give the return as a decimal, then print exactly `Day 1: 4.00%` and `Day 2: -2.00%`.

widget.label: returns.py
widget.starter:
# returns.py: three closing prices, in pounds
p0 = 100.00
p1 = 104.00
p2 = 101.92


def daily_return(old, new):
    # Give back the return as a decimal: 0.04 for +4%.
    return 0.0


r1 = daily_return(p0, p1)
r2 = daily_return(p1, p2)

# Print one line per day, for example:
# print(f"Day 1: {r1 * 100:.2f}%")
widget.solution:
# returns.py: three closing prices, in pounds
p0 = 100.00
p1 = 104.00
p2 = 101.92


def daily_return(old, new):
    return (new - old) / old


r1 = daily_return(p0, p1)
r2 = daily_return(p1, p2)

print(f"Day 1: {r1 * 100:.2f}%")
print(f"Day 2: {r2 * 100:.2f}%")
widget.how: Check runs your script as `python3` would. Test 1 compares everything it prints with the expected output. The other tests try `daily_return` on other prices, so it must work for any two.

feedback.correct: A ten-line script that computes and prints returns: the Stage 0 exit test, passed in the browser. Now run it from your own terminal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test: compare what was expected with what your script gave.

byKey.error: Your script stopped with an error. Read the message from the bottom: what went wrong, then which line.

explain.text: `daily_return` computes $(104.00 - 100.00) \div 100.00 = 0.04$ and $(101.92 - 104.00) \div 104.00 = -0.02$. The f-string multiplies by 100 and keeps two decimals. Because the recipe takes any two prices, the hidden tests could try other days.

items.title: Run it on your own machine
items.prompt:
Do the Stage 0 exit test for real, on your own computer, and write up what you did.

(a) Open a new terminal window. Check your Python: give the command, what it printed, and its minor version.

(b) Make a folder called `stage0`, move the terminal into it, and open it in VS Code. List the three commands in order.

(c) Save your `returns.py` from the last question in `stage0`. Run it from the terminal and copy the command and its output.

(d) Change `p1` to `0.00` and run it again. Read the error from the bottom up: say what went wrong, the line Python stopped on, and the real cause.

(e) A friend installed Python, but in the terminal that was open during the install `python3` gives `command not found`. Explain why, and the fix.
items.model:
**(a)** In a new window: `python3 --version`. It printed `Python 3.12.4` (yours may differ). The minor version is 12: the middle number, read as a whole number. A new window matters, because a window opened before the install may have an old PATH.

**(b)**

```bash
mkdir stage0
cd stage0
code .
```

`mkdir` makes the folder, `cd` moves the terminal into it, and `code .` opens the current folder in VS Code. Its built-in terminal then starts in `stage0`.

**(c)** From `stage0`:

```text
python3 returns.py
Day 1: 4.00%
Day 2: -2.00%
```

The file must be plain text with the `.py` extension, saved in `stage0`, or Python reports `can't open file`.

**(d)** With `p1 = 0.00`, day 1 is $(0 - 100) \div 100 = -1$, which works. Day 2 divides by `p1`, which is now zero:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../stage0/returns.py", line 12, in <module>
    r2 = daily_return(p1, p2)
  File ".../stage0/returns.py", line 8, in daily_return
    return (new - old) / old
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
```

From the bottom: *what* is division by zero. *Where*: Python stopped on line 8, inside `daily_return`, which was called from line 12 for day 2. The *cause* is neither line: it is the `0.00` typed on line 3. A price of zero is bad data, so the fix is the price, not the formula.

**(e)** A terminal window reads the PATH once, when it opens. The installer added Python's folder to the PATH settings after that window had read them. So that window searches the old list of folders, finds no `python3`, and says `command not found`. The fix is to close it and open a new window, which reads the new PATH. Reinstalling is not needed.

rubric.text: Gives `python3 --version` run in a new window, its output, and the minor version as the middle whole number.
Lists `mkdir stage0`, `cd stage0`, `code .` in that order, and says what each does.
Runs `python3 returns.py` from inside `stage0` and shows the two output lines `Day 1: 4.00%` and `Day 2: -2.00%`.
Reads the traceback from the bottom: division by zero, stopped inside `daily_return` called for day 2, real cause the 0.00 price.
Explains that the old window read its PATH before the install, and that opening a new window fixes it.

items.prose: Ana practises on keybr.com for 10 minutes a day, every day, for 6 weeks.
items.question: How many hours of practice is that in total?

widget.label: Hours
widget.accept: 7 hours: 42 days of 10 minutes is 420 minutes.

feedback.correct: 42 sessions of 10 minutes: 420 minutes, or 7 hours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the days, multiply by 10 minutes, then turn minutes into hours.

byKey.minutes: You stopped at minutes. 420 minutes is 420 ÷ 60 = 7 hours.
byKey.weekdays: You counted weekdays only. She practises every day: 7 days a week.

explain.text: 6 weeks is 42 days. 42 × 10 = 420 minutes, and 420 ÷ 60 = 7 hours. Short daily sessions add up, and they build the habit better than one long one.

items.title: A trade script from a blank file
items.prose: Sam bought 40 shares at £12.25 each and later sold all 40 at £13.00. His broker charged a £10.00 fee on the buy and another on the sell. Sam will save your script as `/home/sam/desk/trade.py`. A new terminal on his machine opens in his home folder, `/home/sam`.
items.question: Write `trade.py`. Store `cost`, all Sam paid with the fee, and `proceeds`, what he received after the fee. Store `profit`, proceeds minus cost, and `ret`, profit divided by `cost`. Print one line for each, labelled `Cost:`, `Proceeds:`, `Profit:` and `Return:`, in that order. Begin with comment lines giving the commands that run it from its own folder, in a new terminal.

widget.label: trade.py
widget.starter: # trade.py: Sam's round trip, in pounds
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, each on a fresh run of your script as `python3` would run it. They read your four values and printed lines, then follow the commands in your comments from `/home/sam`.
widget.solution:
# cd ~/desk
# python3 trade.py

# trade.py: Sam's round trip, in pounds
shares = 40
buy = 12.25
sell = 13.00
fee = 10.00

cost = shares * buy + fee
proceeds = shares * sell - fee
profit = proceeds - cost
ret = profit / cost

print("Cost:", cost)
print("Proceeds:", proceeds)
print("Profit:", profit)
print("Return:", ret)

feedback.correct: The script works out the trade and says how to run it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what the first failing test reports, then check that part of your script.

byKey.error: Your script stopped with an error. Read the message from the bottom: what went wrong, then which line.

explain.text: Each fee adds to what Sam paid and comes off what he got: $40 \times 12.25 + 10 = 500$ and $40 \times 13.00 - 10 = 510$. So the profit is £10, and the return is $10 \div 500 = 0.02$. From `/home/sam`, `cd desk` moves to the script's folder, then `python3 trade.py` runs it.
